newsitem.title: UK: Speculators push zinc to new peak, others dull.
newsitem.headline: Speculators push zinc to new peak, others dull.

text.p: Speculative buying thrust LME zinc to fresh 4-3/4 year highs in pre-market activity on Thursday morning, but business was thin in the other metals, traders said.
Three months zinc knocked down resistance at $1,380 per tonne and hit a high of $1,386, the strongest since September 1992. This was up $11 on Wednesday's afternoon kerb close.
"Far Eastern selling came in again as it has over the past few days, but this time the specs took them on," a senior trader said.
Turnover was strong, with 500 lots done already by his firm alone, he added.
In addition to the Far Eastern selling, some longs decided to take profits around $1,385, traders said.
Prices were last indicated at $1,381/83.
The market may be content to consolidate at the higher numbers, with an effort to bolster prices at the end of the day to ensure a close above $1,380, traders added.
Little business was seen in the other metals.
Copper hovered at recent levels under $2,600, but any attempt to break the big number would attract producer selling, traders said.
An increase in stocks of 825 tonnes was not supportive and the market was last at $2,587, down $5.
Support was pegged at Monday's low of $2,565, with resistance at the June 12 peak of $2,609.
The premium of cash of three months held steady at $103/$108, with tightness emerging in September. One dealer said some funds who had been short in July had now rolled it over into September.
Aluminium was also marginally weaker, again shrugging off a sizeable fall in stocks, this time 3,875 tonnes.
It was indicated at $1,588/91, versus Wednesday's close of $1,593.
"There are too many longs in aluminium at the moment," a trader said.
Support was pegged at Tuesday's low of $1,565, with resistance at the 10-day moving average of $1,600 and then at $1,610.
Nickel dipped after stock figures showed a net gain of 1,128 tonnes, bringing the total to 52,542 tonnes.
Prices slipped below $7,200 and settled at $7,150/70, down from a kerb close of $7,230.

"Reports of Russian material having arrived, with more coming into the market, coupled with the low usage of primary nickel in the stainless steel industry, is mitigating the impact of the Inco strike," analyst Martin Squires of broker Rudolf Wolff said.
Lead was barely changed at $624/26 compared to a kerb close of $624, continuing its recovery from Tuesday's dip to 20-month lows.
The bounce was impressive, but the market needed to clear $630 before it was out of danger, Squires said.
Tin and alloy were little changed at $5,570/90 and $1,470/80 respectively.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542-8065
